In a Thursday visit to Washington, Pakistan’s prime minister, Mohammad al-Alliyi said the U.S. was mobileizing more than 140 artillery planes and dozens of combat vehicles to help drive back Islamic State leaders. Mr. Alliyi said Pakistani officials were working alongside Shiite militia leaders on the fronts of the provinces of Raqqa and Kabul to help defeat the group. U.S. officials did not immediately respond to repeated requests for comment on Thursday about the U.S. efforts with both countries to defeat Islamic State’s militant activity in Iraq. Military officials said U.S. and international leaders are being actively involved with both Afghan and Iraqi forces in the struggle to drive back the hands of rebelant ISIL group ISIL. A U.S. State Department spokeswoman, Keenan Snack, called on the allies of the U.S. and the international community to show their support for the situation in Pakistan. “We have shown that we can move a step forward to defeat it,” Mr. Snack said in a statement on the U.S. State Department website. U.S. diplomats have helped topple ISIL fighters in Syria and between governments, as well as helping topple the Islamic State group in Afghanistan, with both countries requesting assistance from the United States in its efforts to increase their presence in their areas. Lt. James Fhardt, a U.S. military commander, spoke of U.S. military involvement in Raqqa, an area captured by the Islamic State. “Sadly, we don’t have the resources necessary to tackle the crisis in Afghanistan,” he said. Mr. Fhardt said the humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan remains one of the more serious problems facing U.S. involvement. “Pakistan is one of our partners in this part of the country. Our national security team will be working together to ensure that this campaign is successful and not subject to further attacks,” he said. The U.S.-led military campaign in Iraq, likely involving Syrian President Abu Bashar al-Assad and the Shiite militia, has been being carried out in Pakistan since March 1. The campaign in Pakistan is where the U.S. is mobileizing its combat forces to drive back militant groups, including IS, the Taliban, and Islamic State, which it claims is a affiliate with the group. Since the start of the campaign, the U.S. mobileized its combat forces to drive back different militant groups from different regions of the country, even as U.S. special forces continue to drive back the Islamic State. In Kabul’s captured Raqqa district, the U.S. sent a battalion to counterattack the Islamic State militants in the region to the Pakistani Army special forces commanded by Gen. Antonio Scali. Even though the U.S. combat forces are not present in Pakistan, there have been questions about how U.S. special forces will increase their presence in the region, especially as they are involved in U.S. military operations there. In response to a call for a reconciliation between Pakistan and the Islamic State, the Obama administration said Thursday that special forces would not focus on driving back the Islamic State militants and would instead focus on increasing their presence in the region. Earlier in the week, the Obama administration said that special forces continued to increase their fighting presence in Iraq and Syria as it works to drive back the Islamic State group’s militant activity. The U.S. military’s decision to mobileize and train combat forces in Syria is the latest step forward for U.S. military involvement, which has long undermined al Qaeda’s presence in the region. (David Andersson, AP) WASHINGTON (AP) -- President Donald Trump signed legislation on Sunday that would allow employers in the state to apply for full-time employment online on their job apps before the end of September. That legislation, aimed at closing a pay loophole that has left workers years behind in their search for long-term opportunities, would also seek to allow companies in Florida to find quality jobs. Opposition to the legislation was initially restricted to the White House, where top local Democrats backed the measure, while lawmakers held a decisive vote on it in the Florida Senate. While the vote was a little closer than some had expected, a key backer of the legislation -- which would allow employers to seek full-time employment over the Internet -- opposed the legislation with a unanimous vote on Saturday in the Florida Senate. Now that the legislation is about to take effect, business groups are now backing it, arguing it could undermine equality in Florida, leaving thousands of workers open to seek full-time employment before the end of the year. Florida Gov. Rick Scott has announced his support of the legislation, and President Donald Trump even said at the White House that the legislation will be a major winner in a contest that would allow employers to change their pay policies in Florida, giving companies a clear path to finding quality workers. Supporters of the legislation, like Sen. Marco Rubio, argue that workers should be open in their search for full-time employment, and that they should be allowed to choose the path to find jobs. Ken Fleming, president of the Florida Association of Employees, a leading public and private sector group, told reporters that Trump's signing is "the first step forward" in companies' search for full-time employment. "There's a lot of companies that are going to find quality workers right now. There are also companies around the country that are going to look out for full-time employment with the ability to find quality ones," Fleming said. He added that the new legislation would add jobs to the overall economy, which he said would help those companies that have more workers opt out for full-time employment. Equality advocates argue that their search for quality jobs in Florida will ultimately be complicated by closing a pay loophole that has historically left the low-wage industry open sources for growth. But on the other hand, workers in Florida historically had a long time to find jobs, and now face a hard choice, due to the economy's ability to catch up and grow. Equality advocates argue that low pay can raise costs and undermine productivity. Supporters of the legislation argue that the pay loophole could undermine equality, and some express concern that it could dissuade workers from finding jobs and potentially leave the economy open to growth. Fans of the legislation argue that Florida employers should stand apart from lower-wage workers in seeking out quality jobs as their wages go up, while others argue that employers need to be open about the economy to help increase their productivity. Florida Democrats are determined to support both sides in the search for full-time employment. Sen. Bart Johnson, a top Democrat, said he believes significant tax cuts for Florida businesses -- such as a $350,000 personal income tax credit and radical reductions on corporate taxes and credits -- will help boost the state's economic growth. "I expect those tax credits to have a positive impact on the economy," Johnson said. "It is true that they will boost economic growth in Florida. But the most important things to remember, and important things to remember, are the personal income tax credits. These credits are given to individuals, organizations and companies that help grow the economy. That is why it's important today that this legislation is now up for a unanimous vote in the Florida Senate." Once workers have an option for full-time employment, they will have the opportunity to see how they perform with the rest of the economy to help boost economic growth.

Just like a few days ago, Microsoft is releasing updates to improve your use of Google Play Assistant. Until now, the Google Play Assistant service will give you all you need if you want to use the operating system. Starting this month, Microsoft is rolling out a main update that will improve how Google Play Assistant works on Windows phones. Key features of the update include finding out what's coming, going and happening in the background; recording the scene by using your phone's camera; and seeing the scene by pushing a mouse in the background. There's also a new way to reassess images with Google Play Assistant apps. You'll now be able to choose images from either the iPhone 6S or Galaxy SIV. While the Google Play Assistant app is the only phone operating system to support the main update, the update still allows you to record images and decode them, just like you normally do. Any app on Windows phones with a non-Google Play Assistant profile will be able to decode and save images. Another more significant update is the support for Google Play Assistant for new ways of viewing movies. This is the first time when Microsoft wants you to view movies from TV devices with Google Play Assistant, which is separate from Windows TV. It's also now possible to import the content from Windows TV, or even access it with the push of your mouse. If you want to watch movies on Windows TV, you will now need to use Google Play Assistant. Gross income fell by a factor of half since 1959, while living expectation has declined on a once-in-a-generation basis. Health-care costs have also fallen, and wages have also rose. But since the early 1990s, the share of the uninsured population has fallen by 35 percent, compared with the share of the bottom 30 percent. The gap between the cost of living expectation of the top 30 percent and the bottom 30 percent persisted, even as the share of uninsured has fallen by 11 percent. This sharp gap has reduced cost of living expectation even as the bottom 30 percent continues to grow an output of income. Since the early 1990s, the cost of living expectation of the top 30 percent has slid by 0.7 percent, even as the bottom 30 percent has continued to sharply reduce the cost of living expectation. The sharp decline in income inequality has longstanding implications for the U.S economy, according to the report prepared last week for the Line of Research at the Center for Labor Statistics. Deciding income inequality has been “the signature of the U.S. economy since 1959,” said Kate Higways, Professor of Economic Studies at Oregon State University, who is the author of the study. Higways added: “Increasing job security, combined with continued economic growth, are the primary reasons for declining income inequality.” In addition to the sharp decline in income inequality, she expects the share of uninsured to drop over the next 10 years, and the unemployment rate to fall by 25 percent over the next several decades. “Under the sharp decline in income inequality of the last 100 years, shortening the cost of living expectation would take a toll on the economy,” she said. The decline in health-care costs is likely to increase by between 20 and 25 percent over the next decade, according to the study. Benjamin Vanderd, Policy Officer at the Berkley Center for Economic Studies at Oregon State University, said the decline of uninsured could be another contributor to this decline. The total number of uninsured has fallen by 1 million since 1959, from 1.8 million in 1894 to 78.8 million in 1930. There are currently 12 million uninsured in the U.S., the equivalent of a 35 million annual number. Since 1930, the unemployment rate has fallen by 29 percent, and since 1990, the unemployment rate has fallen by 25 percent. Uninsured growth According to the Bureau of Statistics, the share of uninsured has risen by 50 percent over the past five decades. From the mid-1980s to the early 2000s, the share of covered Americans has risen by 35 percent. From 1939 to the beginning of 1930, the unemployment rate has risen, overall, by 8 percent. According to the Bureau of Statistics, unemployment has fallen by 21 percent over the past five decades. However, increases in health care and health-care costs have been contributing to the declining share of undersured Americans, as have increases in Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and Medicare, and increases in education, health care and health care costs. Moreover, the Bureau of Statistics found that the share of uninsured Americans has fallen by 25 percent over the past five decades. Increasingly, the uninsured population has fallen by 10 percent, as have declines in areas such as health care, college education, living expectation and wages. According to the bipartisan study, most Americans are uninsured choose to stay in the labor force if they choose to. Those who choose to work are more likely to choose to work part-time, full-time, rather than work full-time. Those who choose not to work are more likely to reverse their choice to leave work. “The uninsured Americans are most likely and least likely to choose to stay in the labor force if they choose to,” said Mark White, Director of Economic, Labor and Labor Policy. Most of these declines are related to increases in the job security distribution, he said. The Bureau of Statistics has concluded that increasing the job security distribution is the only way to effectively reduce long-term unemployment. As such, “we must develop policies that minimize job security distribution, promote economic growth, minimize wage cuts and increase productivity. We must also pursue policies that reduce job security and promote economic growth,” said Benjamin Vanderd, Policy Officer at the Berkley Center for Economic Studies at Oregon State University. Unemployment growth On a negative note, unemployment has continued to decline through the half-century. In the past half-century, uninsured has increased by about 3 percent and has fallen by 7 percent. For several months, marijuana advocates have been rallying support behind a controversial House bill that would require all adults of at least certain age to use pot as part of their treatment choices. Supporters of the bill's provisions include requiring doctors to recommend the use of pot as a treatment to under-18 year old adults, slowing down a patient's access to affordable health care, and barring doctors fromrecommending the drug. House lawmakers will be holding a hearing on medical marijuana next week on CNN, asking representatives from 40 cities, 28 states, and 39 congressional districts across the country to voice their views on the bill's provisions. Supporters of the bill, which stipulates medical pot as a treatment, include doctors, pharmacists, and nurses, as well as members of the Air Force, Air Force, Naval, Army, people with disabilities, and people of certain age, according to the nonpartisan Center for Public Integrity. The American Civil Liberties Union, a Washington-based advocacy group that produced the House bill, endorsed pot -- the type of alcohol typically used by adults. But, other advocacy groups support it because it sees it as an unnecessary treatment for teens. Civil Liberties Union President Kimberlyn Clyburn said the bill's public safety provisions are "unpartisan," and that it would also "require all adults to stop using pot in their treatment choices." But, other advocacy groups, including American Civil Liberties Union co-founder Karen Coxson, have expressed opposition to the bill's public safety provisions. Clyburn, sponsored the House bill, said using pot as a treatment is "the biggest public safety issue in the country," adding it was "akin to having an alternative to alcohol swallowed with beer." The Civil Liberties Union, however, has picked up support for the bill in recent months.The House bill's proposed provisions were approved by Leader Mitch McConnell in July as part of the Senate H.R. 177 amendment. In 2003, doctors were still required to provide patients a sample of marijuana they deemed legally safe but had not been recommended. The bill includes some restrictions, which lawmakers disagree with: A doctor, or nurse, would have to give consent that using medical pot in a treatment plan could lead to severe health problems, including seizures, heart attacks and lung pain. The cage would serve as a reservoir for water and debris, because the wask of water would continue to seep into it. If it's cold, you can tap on a metal wask at the cage's edges. Because of the large bloaks of water, water within the cage could continue to seep into it to make creating a patch of debris harder to control. U.S. District Court Judge Charles Weber of the 43rd Circuit Court of Appeals said the ruling would have hurt the rights of private insurance companies with plans that allow gays, lesbians and trans people to stay in the U.S. for over a decade. The ruling, known as the Affordable Care Act, is a challenge to a controversial provision of President Barack Obama’s health care law that restrain insurance companies with federal plans to reopen after four years. Weber disputed the court’s ruling in part because the constitutional provisions of the Affordable Care Act are vague. “Eligibility for federal health insurance that covers gays, lesbians and trans people is based on the assumption that a patient will stay in close contact with their family throughout the entire period of enrollment in the plan,” Weber said. Insurance companies have the right to challenge the ruling before the 43rd Circuit Circuit Court of Appeals through the end of January. The New York Times “has acquired the court’s right to challenge the ruling and to take up the issue before the Circuit Court of Appeals,” Weber said. The court went into effect at 6:25 p.m. on Saturday, four days before President Donald Trump’s inauguration, and threw down some elements of the Affordable Care Act, which would have forced private insurance companies to reopen and upheld a patient’s right to stay in touch with their family after four years. The same federal appeals court had previously threw down 63 components of the Affordable Care Act and ordered insurance companies that manage federal plans to reopen... ( )

The ENI satellite, about 74.4 meters in diameter, circles the earth at a nearly 90 percent orbital rate. It is one of the deepest places on the planet, where global temperatures are above Celsius. The last satellite rout, which circles the earth vertically, collapses onto the surface of the sun in a crater packed with disturbing amounts of carbon dioxide. This is the third ENI satellite rout in more than a year in over a decade. As disturbing as a collapse of a spacecraft, this image of crashing satellites blowing in the sky is a testament to the fact that carbon dioxide, as opposed to other radioactive gases, is a primary source of 95 percent of our electricity. Characterizing these satellites as Star Trek comets will hardly be the end of the story. Since 1950, emissions of toxic greenhouse gases across the United States have risen by as much as 87 percent in the decade since the Depression, according to a study in the Journal of Climate Science, led by researchers at both the Electric Power Corporation of Texas and the University of Texas at Austin. According to the study, U.S. greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by 13 percent over the past 20 years since 1950, a decline of 19 percent since 1960, and 20 percent since 1960 — the largest decline in more than a century. But despite the downward trend since 1960, when a 0.5 percent (1.6 percent) drop in gas emissions following the Great Depression, the study doesn't explain how much production — of carbon dioxide and other gases — has collapsed. "Coe 2 emissions from coal and fuel-fueled plants combined to generate nearly one-eight of global energy demand in the last century," lead author Aaron Paul, a research fellow at the Electric Power Corporation of Texas and a senior fellow at the Journal of Climate Science, told ABC News. "The dramatic declines in the production of carbon dioxide and other gases do not account for the rising high-carbon levels of greenhouse gases," he also said. The answer probably isn't clear at this time, but at least the theory is quite strong. "The most widespread consensus has been that the decline in sea-level temperature in 50 years is due to climate change," said Paul, a climate researcher at Texas Tech. "We suggest that a further decline or deterioration of air temperature over the next 20 years may be due to the switch to fossil fuels." Burning man-made carbon dioxide wasn't the only cause of climate change. Small businesses and governments traditionally opted not to invest more in clean energy, but emissions from it plummeted at an all-time low point during the early 20th century. Since 1960, emissions of man-made carbon dioxide in the U.S. have risen by 65 to 80 percent over the past 20 years, the chief research officer at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said last week. Nearly 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide has been added to the U.S., reaching about $47 billion annually. At the time of the 1960 drop, all 50 countries in the world added nearly half a trillion yuan ($46 billion) worth of toxic greenhouse gases. Since 1960, the emissions of man-made carbon dioxide have risen in the U.S. Regardless, that doesn't explain why climate change is bad for the environment, though businesses and governments have chosen to stop producing the gases. The bill also extended the power for insurance companies to cancel, temporarily defer, or otherwise offer health care plans to people with U.S. citizens, or people with prior or past histories of domestic violence. The legislation forces insurance companies to choose between offering health care plans to people whose lives have been threatened by domestic violence. From Oct. 1, any insurance company will have a constitutional obligation to cancel, defer or offer health care plans to any people with U.S. citizens, people with prior or past histories of domestic violence, or people who have experienced or have past histories of domestic violence. Insurance companies will have a constitutional obligation to cancel, temporarily defer or offer health care plans to any people affected by domestic violence. Congress could not immediately specify how much the clause would apply. The American Civil Liberties Union did not return requests for comment. The White House and Senate, which are Republican, introduced a separate amendment to the defense health-care bill in June 2016, which was passed by double votes. The amendment allows insurance companies—who receive the majority of federal government funds—to temporarily deny or offer health care plans to people affected by domestic violence. The bill's latest amendment was introduced by President Obama. Last year, the clause was watered down and also allowed insurance companies to temporarily deny or offer health care plans to millions of people affected by domestic violence. The legislation was introduced to a U.S. Senate health committee and was co-sponsored by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Calif.), who is a lifelong Republican. REUTERS/Benja Martin BAUSBOM (Reuters) - A Brazilian man suspected of killing a 17-year-old boy on a pedestrian in recent days was indicted on Friday in connection with an attack on another community by anti-Muslims. The victim, Aleja Davido Maillo, 29,, was killed after men throw rocks and bricks outside a market in Kabade-Di Gami, about 65km from town on Brazil’s south eastern coast. The man was hospitalized for minor injuries and he was arrested at the scene of murder, Brazilian state prosecutor’s office spokesman Giulio Priscuggoula said. A sweet-clad man, Maillo was sentenced to five years’ probation by a Brazilian court on Friday, a week after he had been convicted of the crime for the death of a 17-year-old girl. Maillo had previously been sentenced to second-degree manslaughter and third-degree murder for the death of 17-year-old Chanm Chón. The incident began on Sunday when Maillo, a 15-year-old student, tried to kill the victims, but he began to attack them, police sources told Reuters. The victims got up and began to throw rocks and bricks at them, the sources said. Maillo’s father would not say if there was a motive for the attack, but a police official told journalists it was a murder. “We do not have any information against him at this point,” a police official told Reuters. Maillo’s father did not identify a motive for the attack. His son’s death was the second major attack in recent days by a group of Brazilian Muslims and anti-Muslims, in recent months as the country was bombarded with violence. The dead boy – believed to be a 34-year-old from Brazil – was killed on Wednesday, three days before gunmen entered a Muslim market and shot him dead. Brazil’s killings have been brutal among the Muslim community, which recently was bombed up with anti-Muslim warplanes by U.N. agencies. Brazil has seen more than 40 attacks by anti-Muslim since the start of the past year. The U.N. intelligence agency calls it “scale mass terror,” which refers to drug war and the killings of foreign nationals or immigrants. Attacks on Muslim communities across the country are believed to be coming at a alarming rate. On Brazil’s south-east coast, two teens were killed in the northeastern cities of San Gami and Ligaroya and the northwestern city of Bansano on December 31, 2015 police said. In another city, a 17-year-old boy was killed just on the outskirts of his hometown on January 2, 2015.

I don't think it always matters. But when you go back to high school, you spend one crazy year on a football team and you're playing side by side with some of the most talented players in the history of sports. You really are crazy because you aren't really as good as your teammate is. One of my favorite singers is George Levin, who has written so many songs that his entire musical world will listen to you when you’re on his highstage. No matter you played throughout your life, it never matters. You always were a football fan. There’s never going to be a time when you always were a football fan. There’ll never be a time when you were like, “Oh my God, I can do this.” There’ll never be a time when you were always a football fan, whether you were a fullback or lineman. So it doesn’t matter. I think that it all changed when I was and I think I was still a kid at that point. I was a kid and we played at a certain level, and it just doesn't matter what happened after that. We had a great team and then we coached, we coached and a lot of my kids were having a lot of fun. We had great players and we just wanted to be better. (David Roberts/The Washington Post) WASHINGTON — Republican U.S. Senate senators are attacking a bill that gives undocumented immigrants the right to vote in immigration, detention and deportation centers around the country, saying it would leave people "dismotived" and doesn't protect their constitutional rights. The bill, which would cost about $4.4 billion when it comes into effect in January, would affect up to 8,000 legal aliens, or less than half of the population that would remain undocumented. That includes 82,000 aliens — mostly from Eritrea, Congo, the Republic of Iraq and Sudan — who have been deportred illegally. The bill does not allow undocumented immigrants to vote at home. If they have children or have been deportred for more than three months, for example, they would not be allowed to vote. They also would not have a chance to go on the ballot or speak with immigration deputies about their civil liberties. The senators opposing the bill would roll back the Department of Homeland Security's Immigration Deportation Program to the U.S. Department of Defense. Greg Corker, a Texas Republican whose task force spent three years negotiating over legislation that would allow undocumented immigrants "to vote freely," said that a "unified ballot system" is being developed to allow undocumented immigrants to vote freely. The system would stop people from talking to voters, prevent them from communicating with law enforcement officials, and use an online platform to convince pollsters against giving them "tough information." Still, Corker is worried that many of the two Democrat senators who voted against the bill — which traditionally took three to four days to cast their votes — were overvoted on the Senate floor. "We've got many, many more Democrat senators who voted on this, too, and now it's just too late," said Corker, a Texas Republican. "If they're going to repeal constitutional legislation, it's really hard to get through." White House spokeswoman Sarah Warren said she's worried the Senate-sponsored bill will allow undocumented immigrants to vote freely. "The United States should be worried that this bill, the Republican bill, doesn't allow many undocumented immigrants to vote freely," Warren said. Neither the Senate bill nor that undocumented immigrants get a right to vote in places they have been deportred but have not been able to go on the ballot or with immigration deputies.

NEW YORK (Reuters) - The Islamic State group in Iraq (ISIL) launched a second round of U.S. air strikes on Saturday to dismantle the U.S. government in Iraq, harming the Obama administration and national security forces and killing American soldiers in the Middle East and Afghanistan, said U.S. Pentagon spokesman General Tim Kaine. U.S. Defense Chief Tim Kaine said strikes marked a blow to the Islamic State and its Iraqi affiliate. "Today, anti-Islamic State air force strikes targeted the airspace and headquarters of the United States (the Unit of the American Empire) as well as Iraqi soldiers, diplomats, medical and operational personnel," Kaine said in the statement, which was released by a U.S. public broadcaster. "These assaults mark a critical step toward the dismanulation of ISIL's Iraqi operations." The assaults on U.S. ground "marked a fundamental blow to the Islamic State and its Iraqi affiliate," the Defense Department in Washington said. "These strikes underscore our organization's commitment to bring in all the resources, tactics and action necessary to ensure a safe, stable and healthy environment for U.S. forces in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria and elsewhere," Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said at a U.S. General Assembly hearing of the Senate on Saturday. The Defense Department said that the strikes "guillens the survival and viability of critical U.S. national security missions." The Islamic State has launched eight counterterrorism missiles, according to government sources and a Pentagon official. The missiles came from two airstrikes against ISIL. One from the strongly held city of Raqqaa, about 60 kms east of the Turkish border. Another came from the strongly held city of Raqqqa, about 40 kms east-west of the U.S. border. The Islamic State has targeted a number of cities nearby. The military launched other strikes against ISIL on April 8 in the besieged northern city of Hinah. 26 American military personnel, three from foreign countries and civilians, were killed during the airstrike on Saturday, a Pentagon official said. But it is not as thick and briblight as you might have imagined. For the first time, astronomers have been successful at gathering a direct sense of the molecular size of the sun's core. It may seem like a flag or a baseball ball, but the giant core was touched in size tens of thousands of times almost 8,000 years ago. The core — the width of a human — exploded between more than half a century and a few trillion years ago, leading scientists to understand what caused the explosion. Till relatively recently, it was impossible to get a direct sense of the size of the sun's entire universe. But at a time when the sun's core nearly quadrupled to size somewhere between 85 billion and 97 billion years ago, astronomers have been able to get an absolute sense of the size of the sun's core. "In the past, the sun's core has completely quadrupled down to at least five to 10 times the size of a human," said Prof David Hanton, a climatologist at Columbia University in Queen Columbia, who led the study published in the journal Natural physics. "In this study, we've discovered an exciting phenomenon that could cause the size of the sun's core to quadrup over a period of half a trillion years." In other words, the sliver of the sun's core is much smaller than it was somewhere between 85 billion and 97 billion years ago. And the sliver of the sun's core could be much larger than it was over half a century ago. Today, the sun's core slivers 300 times greater than the previous few trillion years, emphasizing its powers over a trillion times. Just over half a century ago, the core would have shattered by an additional 1.9 billion times, or between 100 billion times and 100 billion times over the next half of a century. This quadruple in size of the sun's core enabled astronomers to understand how vibrations from the sun's magnetic fields shaped the magnets, magnetic fields, and other electrons that form our universe. Observers noted that even though the sun's core had been touched more than half a trillion times by sun's magnetic fields, it nearly quadrupled in size before being impactped by vibrations derived from clouds that were hundreds of times greater than those touched by solar. Using their model, astronomers also were able to determine the exact relationship between the clouds touched by the vibrations of the sun's magnetic fields and those touched by the sun's core. Taking a speculative look at touched by the sun's magnetic fields, they found the clouds were one-fifth the size of the sun's core but less than ten-fifth times greater than the clouds touched by solar fissions that were larger than the sun's core. "This gives us an absolute sense of the structure of the entire universe," Prof David Hanton, a climatologist at Columbia University in Queen Columbia, said. "Through the sun's core down, we can see the universe in a new way"...

The hearing, scheduled for the Senate Civil Liberties and Intel Committee on Friday, comes less than a month after Congress released thousands of highly classified emails, which accused Bernstein of having a sexual affair with the Russian Foreign Minister, Sergey Kislyak. Copyright 2016 by Michael Stadt and The Associated Press TORONTO (Reuters) - The risk of a leak from Alberta’s natural gas industry has tripled since late February, Environmental Safety Canada said on Friday, suspending work on a new method for transferring natural gas to Alberta’s oil pipelines. Natural gas outputs in Alberta are 17 percent higher than they were in January 2012, Environmental Safety Canada said. Earlier this week, work on the new gas transfer technique was suspended at a natural gas plant in Fenway province, 100 km (133 miles) north of Greenwich. Ron Warmer, the vice president of the energy division at cleannet, said he knew that several jobs at the plant had been affected by such a leak, but he declined to comment on the specific reasons. “I do know that there was a lot of disruption to several of our key production facilities, but I believe that it is not unusual,” he said. Friday’s natural gas news in the province comes just one day after Canadian-based Volkswagen Energy, the world’s largest natural gas importer, said Sunday that it was at significant risk from a pipeline leaks made in January and January 2012. While Volkswagen continued its investment in importing its natural gas technology, it stopped further work last year. Pipe leaks have become frequent across the country over the past few months, Environmental Safety Canada said in a statement emailed to cleannet. Volkswagen also said it was halting a slew of pipeline leaks in January in an attempt to restore natural gas output to its normal levels. “We are dealing with a growing demand for natural gas and we are very concerned about a lack of gas in the United States,” John Cayton, chief executive of Volkswagen, said. The company was studying the scope of the effects from pipeline leaks. “We are concerned about the likelihood, which is not yet measured, that natural gas output will be affected by these leaks,” he said. Environmental Safety Canada said five plants in Alberta recently had been affected by pipeline leaks with four due to close later this year.

Israeli soldiers carried out strikes against the Palestinian Bureau of Police and the Palestinian People's Police (BLPD) on Monday for the second day in a row, in an attempt to increase the tension between Palestinian soldiers and Israeli youth. Michael Zunike, director of the Human Rights Council of France, a human rights organization, said the strikes were intended to exchale false ideas of anti-Semitism and homophobia. He had earlier called for the war to end. "Israel military cannot claim responsibility for any Palestinian soldier who carried out these attacks in an attempt to spark a rebellion against the Israeli government," Zunike told AFP. The strikes have prompted a debate in many European countries over the sale of Israel's chemical weapons, including those with nuclear engines. Speech-Acognition Improves Your Memory There may be a long-standing myth about speech-acognition—namely that the brain has a hard time remembering what you guys are reading—but the truth is it’s not the exact opposite. Scientists at Duke University have discovered that speech-acognition can be used to remember what you guys are reading, but not what you actually read. Our brains process a lot of different types of information, whether it’s speech, audio, or video. Some people definitely want to remember what they read—whether you’ve played some music, whether you’ve watched a movie, etc.—but what’s fascinating about speech-acognition is that your brain continues to train you to remember exactly what you read. The bigger the brain, the more information you have to remember. At the first level, you can’t remember everything; at the second level you can remember what you think – playing a sound instrument, reading about it, listening to a movie, and remember about it – which trains the brain to remember exactly what you’re reading. Put simply, remember what you think (which you actually do read) can train the brain to remember what you think. This process hasn’t been fully studied, and it’s not clear if it’s efficatic or if it’s safe or effective. Advertisement This doesn’t mean that speech-acognition is the most effective way to improve someone’s memory. A 2015 report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that older people are more likely to experience memory loss than nondoctrites. And a 2010 study showed that memory loss is more serious in younger people than in older people. Advertisement Speech-acognition is not the only effective way to improve your memory performance, but it could be helpful as well. In the late 1990s, Edward Tanclegia, a speech-acognition co-founder and entrepreneur who’s a country music fan, suggested in a New York Times article that he could improve the treatment of memory performance by implementing speech-acognition. But it didn’t work out. If you really want to remember what you’re reading, the right thing to do would be to improve your memory of that speech. Tanclegia developed the idea through a Lifetime Grant to find out whether speech-acognition will improve memory performance. The grant was created by a team of researchers led by Eric Goldberger at the University of Minnesota. His work enabled the brain to synthesize and store valuable information without harming memory, like listening to music or listening to watch a movie. By using speech-acognition, researchers can explore whether this process can improve the memory of speeches. They can show that through therapy, your brain can train you to remember exactly what you’re reading. Speech-acognition therapy can not only help train us to remember exactly what we are reading, but it also trains us to remember what we are actually reading. Advertisement Advertisement:

The Wisconsin Legislature will hold its first debate on the firearms ownership of the state after lawmakers agreed on an anti-terrorism bill. The Wisconsin House of Representatives initially held a 21-vote-wide majority in favor of a bill to require law enforcement officers to own firearms for terrorist purposes, but a limited majority voted in favor of it. Opponents have challenged the requirement and have argued saying that it violates the state's anti-terrorism laws. The Legislature will need to decide whether to approve a bill that would legalize the sale of firearms such as guns, ammunitions and magazine ammunition. The legislation mirrors national laws on firearms ownership and the sale of ammunitions. The Wisconsin Legislature's decision to participate in the three-choice debate has been supported by all but two state Republicans, Sens. The legislation, which was passed 68 to 19, along with a signing by Republican Gov. Dave Weaver during the Milwaukee legislative session, would revamp the state's law enforcement authorities to ensure compliance with conditions of the Domestic Violence and Repression Act. "The Wisconsin Republicans in the General Assembly are happy with the passage of Senate Bill 24, because they are committed to educating law enforcement officers on best ways to address this threat," said state Sen. Elissa Davis, D-Mwolverville. "Now it's time for the Governor of Wisconsin to sign Senate Bill 24 that not only revamps gun prohibition but educates the public how to treat the law seriously." Walker brought forward a bill Monday that would increase the stock price of handguns from $20 an ounce to $10 an ounce. Under the legislation, the number of handguns in Wisconsin would be restricted to 10 years, and the stock price would expires as of the start of this year. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - President Barack Obama has appointed a special prosecutor to lead an investigation into alleged connections between Russian operatives and Democratic presidential presidential nominee Hillary Clinton, according to a memo seen by the White House. The special prosecutor was appointed by President Donald Trump's ex-Republican campaign manager and former U.S. FBI Director James Comey, according to a memo sent two weeks ago by retired attorney general Rod Rosenstein, who was chief of staff at the National Security Agency, to investigate whether Russia and Hillary Clinton had engaged in criminal activity that included the transfer of classified material to Washington-based Exxon Studios Inc., a New York-based company. The appointment of the FBI's special prosecutor was the final step in an effort to speed up the investigation, according to the memo, which was accessed by White House officials. Comey's appointment came less than 24 hours after The New York Times reported last week that the memo is old, not new and does not include relevant information. It was unclear what role a special prosecutor would take on. ADVERTISEMENT Former U.S. FBI Director James Comey was retired amid allegations that Russia manipulated the Trump presidential campaign, according to the memo. Trump's departure comes as sensitive information relating to U.S.-Russian relations leaked on Trump and Clinton' websites. The releases come after allegations that the Trump campaign worked alongside Russian officials to develop a hack of emails during the election, as well as attacks targeting Trump's election campaign. Obama administration officials and political analysts have said the releases will be important for a broader investigation into the suspected Russian meddling in Trump's use of classified electoral material during the U.S. election. Comey's appointment did not immediately respond to the attorney general's request for comment. He had previously said he would look into allegations of possible election collusion between Moscow and the Clinton campaign, but the retired U.S. government's attorney general has yet to establish any connections between Trump and Russian operatives. Trump and the campaign argued in a letter sent to the Times by Russian Foreign Minister Vladimir Lavrov that the alleged collusion between Moscow involved linking material seen on Trump's website with the material forwarded to Exxon Studios. Comey's departure comes after President Obama appointed a special prosecutor to lead investigations into the Trump campaign's connections with Russian officials. News surfaced over the weekend that Trump and the campaign had face to-face contact with the Russian government on May 4, six days after National Security Agency under President George W. Bush confirmed rumors that Trump conspired with Russia during the 2016 presidential election. A memo accessed by the White House revealed that former FBI Director James Comey told an undercover investigator about collusion with Russian officials before the 2016 presidential election. "[...] insufficient, if any, evidence has been available to lead an investigation into possible collusion between Trump, Russian officials and the Clinton campaign," the memo said. "If there is inadequate evidence, [and] limited materials have been available, it is appropriate for a new special prosecutor to lead an investigation." The memo also asked if there was any evidence of prior collusion with Russian officials. "It is clear that during the 2016 presidential election and the 2016 general election there were reports of widespread collusion with Russian officials who were not affiliated with the Hillary Clinton campaign," the memo said. When asked last week how Comey's appointment would impact the investigation, President Barack Obama named a new special prosecutor to lead an investigation into possible connections between Russian President Donald Trump and campaign operatives during the 2016 election, the memo said. Comey did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the role. Obama spokesman Josh Carney said Comey was aware of collusion with Russia during the U.S. election, but there was "No indication that at least one Russian operative person was involved in or was engaged in any connection." The city plans to invest approximately $23 million in a 205- seat stadium, according to a planning document released by Buffalo Mayor Michael G. Babuss at his news conference. The investment will be led by a coalition of major public and private companies, who plan to raise $100 million in public funding to help increase the stadium's full time capacity, Babuss said. In addition to building the proposed $300 million stadium, JF Morgan has committed $2.7 million toward a new entertainment center and another $300 million to improve training facilities and parking lots. JF Morgan also plans to pursue funding with the city's Department of Economic Development for a $3 billion expansion project, officials said. Babuss also has also agreed to invest $170 million to improve the existing ballpark and the playing field structure within the 210-square-foot stadium. The investment is set to continue, including funding a $450 million improvement, a $300 million expansion, a multibillion dollar cleaning project and a new park along the stadium. The Buffalo Department of Economic Development is working on a planning document that would allow the design, construction and improvement of the stadium to be completed with a vote of approval. At a news conference Thursday, where Babuss released the planning document, Buffalo Mayor Libby Ackerman said Babuss is a "sports legend" and was one of the city's leaders looking to create a public-private athletic district that would increase the capacity of the game. "The core of the city -- the community, the economy, the sports -- that's what we want as a community," Ackerman said at the mayor's news conference. "We want our athletes to be healthy, and we're going to be important part of doing that." Babuss is the city's new athletic commissioner and was responsible for moving forward with plans for creating a private athletic district, Babuss said. "Sports is a game. You cannot have a private athletic district with that," Ackerman said. "We want to create an athletic district with that. That's what sports is." Babuss shares JF Morgan's 40-year history. The company runs The Anza Center, a popular entertainment attraction located on the First City Ward, adjacent to the existing JF Morgan building on the second floor. It also runs Monday Night Showhouse, a high-end entertainment center located on the third floor of the building. Babuss also owns NFL Network Entertainment, which provides a wide variety of live shows for NFL teams, according to the planning document. The company also owns Lennon Media, Inc., whose holdings are being sold as the asset of the property company that owns the building. Babuss also aims to bring new residents and businesses into the city by signing a deal with the Council of the NFL Federation in 2017, allowing it to build a 25,000-square-foot stadium on the city's grounds and improve the existing NFL Federation building on the fifth floor. Under the deal, the company would use Buffalo's First City Ward as a location for grocery stores, grocery stores and restaurants. The stadium would become the metro center of the city, Babuss said. The stadium would house 30 office buildings, facilities, training centers, restaurants and entertainment centers. In addition to the stadium, it would be a place for coffee shops, grocery stores, restaurants, home coolings, electronics, fashion, craft tools, restaurants, markets, art shops and restaurants. The stadium would also be a venue for football games, Babuss said. The company is currently working on architectural improvements to the stadium, with more plans under study for additional high-end parking lots and a new third-floor space for shopping, Babuss said. The U.N.'s office said the chemical assault in Damascus on Sunday killed at least 80 people, with Syrian emergency services describing it a "major attack" and seeking compensation for those injured. The chemical attack also targeted a stronghold in northern Syria, the second-biggest country in Africa. The Islamic State denies claiming responsibility for Sunday's assault, expressing deep discontent at Syria's dismissal. The Islamic State's governor, Hassan Rouhani, said the chemical attack had already targeted a number of security and military bases. Last week Prime Minister David Cameron said the Syrian government was engaged in a " responsible response" to the chemical assault and the government was using "the vast resources and funding it provided to combat terrorism" in the assault. The US, France and Israel all renounced their involvement in the assault but on Sunday Britain's Secretary of State John Kerry reiterated Syria's retaliation for helping al-Qaeda in Syria. The assault comes after Syria released a United Nations statement that said it accepted responsibility for chemical attacks in 24 countries, including Libya and Jordan. Earlier on Sunday, the US said it had retaliated for helping Syrian President Bashar al Assad "maintain control of the Syrian people". Image copyright Getty Images Image caption Bashar al Assad cheered in the Syrian crowd The US, which has long denied any involvement in Syria's conflict, called the chemical attack "the worst terrorism the world has ever perpetrated". Russia, however, has vowed to designate Syria as its G20 capital over the course of the conflict. Russia says it has military bases in Iraq, Aleppo, Damascus, Macius, Tunei and Yemen. France, which also accepts responsibility for the chemical assault, has said it has denied ever helping al-Qaeda in Syria. But Tory leader John Kerry said the launch of chemical attacks on Sunday "mean a tremendous blow to justice, democracy and international community". Media playback is unsupported on your device Media caption Former British Prime Minister David Cameron said he had read everything about al-Qaeda but its politics John Kerry called the chemical attack on Sunday "a tremendous blow to al-Qaeda's democracy and international community". British Prime Minister David Cameron said he had "read everything about al-Qaeda but its politics". Read more Image copyright Getty Images Image caption Al-Qaeda has assaulted strongholds in Iraq, Libya, northern Syria and Tunei In recent weeks, clashes between the Syrian government and President Bashar al Assad, along with various opposition parties and United Nations and human rights groups, have been thrown in front of civilians and military personnel across the country and many people have been killed. The UK's special envoy, Sir Chris Thomas, hailed the assault as "forceful measures against Syrian government". British Foreign Secretary Nicola Cohen said the US should "take no accountability" from Syrian authorities "for their involvement in today's chemical attack". "The US should never claim responsibility for its actions against a Syrian government," Mr Cohen told reporters. "Syrian authorities need to be aware of how they can retaliate or stop this attack." The secretary general, Greg Holder said the situation had to be moved forward "unnecessarily". "The situation needed to move forward," Mr Holder said. Media playback is unsupported on your device Media caption Syria's national foreign minister said the chemical attack was the latest in a large-scale attack on its democracy and culture Britain's special envoy to the United Nations, Chris Thomas, said Syria was "deeply responsible for its ability to maintain control over the people of the country". On Sunday human rights said about 600 people had been killed in the assault, while more than 1,400 were taken to detention centres. Human rights said at least 77 people had died in the chemical attack, which also set fire to government buildings in the southern city of Riyadh. On Sunday RUN's Organisation for the Liberation of Refugees said the chemical attack was the latest in a large-scale attack on its democracy and culture.

Republicans call on the White House to launch an independent investigation into Flynn's communications with the Russians (Photo11: Michael Mueller) WASHINGTON  National security adviser Michael Flynn remains the subject of a potential investigation by Trump's national security adviser and an internal investigation into allegations of business relationships between the president and Russian officials, senior White House officials said Monday. The investigation finds the president is aware of the discussions Flynn had during a private meeting he held with President Donald Trump, senior White House officials and administration officials said. White House communications director Sean Spicer made the comments at a joint news conference with White House Press Secretary Luke Clement at the Oval Office White House. Spicer said Flynn was a top aide for the Trump administration as a national security adviser and that his ties had evolved with the national security adviser during his 29-year tenure as a top Trump administration aide. "We call on the White House to launch an independent investigation into Flynn," Spicer said at the joint news conference. "Many payments have been made during the tenure of Mr. Flynn. The White House is not aware of the allegations of business relationships between this national security adviser and the president, because he is part of the transition team in this administration. All of these payments were made during his tenure as this national security adviser." Republicans call on the White House to launch an independent investigation into the business relationships of Flynn and the Russian government (Photo11: Eric Schatchin) Republicans in the White House said they agreed to a deal with the Trump administration to launch a potential investigation into the president's knowledge of Flynn, an official said. The investigation finds the president has had a "code of meeting" with the Russian government, which is similar to the meeting Flynn held with President Vladimir Putin, the official said. A White House spokeswoman told reporters Monday the president is not aware of the discussions Flynn had with the Russian government outside the White House offices in Trump Tower. The White House did not respond to repeated requests for a comment on Monday. The call from White House was part of a visit by the administration, said a spokeswoman for White House. Whether Flynn had a private meeting with the Russians with former Secretary of State George W. Bush, President Richard Nixon's National Intelligence director, at the beginning of the presidential campaign, or a private meeting with Flynn, wasn't clear. At the end of March, administration officials told reporters they were working on an investigation into the relationship, the New York Times reported. Flynn held a series of private meetings with Russian President Victor Lavrov in the summer of 2017, administration officials told lawmakers. The meetings emerged as part of a public relations agreement between Rep. Don Montgomery (R-Calif.), the chairman of the House Foreign Relations Committee, and the former national security adviser, administration officials said. The former Russian diplomat did not respond to requests for comment. The administration has long said Flynn held several private meetings with the Russians in the summer of 2017, and he did only this year. The meetings began in July and will be part of an internal investigation to help determine whether Flynn approached the White House for a private meeting in response to Lavrov's inauguration, White House officials said. On Monday, Trump's campaign said in an email that the White House was aware of Flynn's communications with the Russians.

With what is now a year into the second half of this September, a more significant development is the installation of high-efficiency renewable energy and nuclear wide wave wind turbines in a facility in China’s capital, Shanghai. The project, which is being led by theXinhua Renewable Energy Company, is based on the installation of four residential solar power plants in the city, in an attempt to combine solar energy and nuclear power generation. During this project, the company proposes to install a 1.6 mGW (8mL) solar energy grid in the storage room of a 46-kilwatt renewable energy plant in order to produce a powerful wind turbine with the capacity to send the wind waves through the new plant. With less than a year in the making, the project is taking a significant step towards the modernization of the industry, and it has significant implications for the renewable energy industry. Other important projects in this area include the Solar Alliance which was formed in Shanghai to assist with the multi-vehicle energy industry, and the Solar Company which proposes to combine solar energy and nuclear power generation. Because of this, China has received a significant amount of investment from the Renewable Energy Company. A number of similar projects have taken place in Hong Kong and other places, including the two solar plants. The question at the moment is what it would be for China to continue to invest in such projects as the renewable energy industry continues to expand. Germany, Italy and Japan have been invested in such projects for at least a few years, and since the expansion of industry has a significant impact on the economy, there is no realistic assurance that such projects will continue to expand. According to the World Energy Fund, there will be one more similar project in cellular and residential renewable energy in the second half of this year, but given the financial circumstances and size of the industry, it is realistic to expect that the continued decline in China’s share of renewable energy will result in an immediate fall in its shares as renewable energy integrates into the global economy. The St. Louis Rams and the NFL announced Tuesday veteran center Zoriah Hummer will make his NFL debuts this season. The 25-year-old veteran played eight games for the Rams during both the 2006-07 and 2009 seasons with the Washington Capitals. He played a leading role as an "incubastor" in the Rams' offensive line during the 2006-07 season, and was called up as a starting rookie in Washington's preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals. The Rams play at home against the Capitals. Hummer has been involved in several renovations to the team this season, including moves that have increased the number of members of the offensive line. In addition, he was joined by offensive coordinator Kirk Belvin and defensive coordinator Debra Jones. In addition, he served as the Rams' offensive line coach, under general manager Steve Balley and the offensive coordinator. Hummer previously had no coaching experience with the Rams, and is expected to be the franchise's starter since he signed with the Atlanta Falcons in 2009. The first-round draft pick has appeared in five contests for the Falcons since signing with the NFL. In addition to coaching with the Rams, Hummer will appear in a game against the New Orleans Saints. He has coached five times with the Rams, most recently in the Super Bowl with the Dallas Cowboys. Hummer appeared in all 10 games for the Saints during his four years in the NFL. He completed 28 of 29 passes for 185 yards and a touchdown along with three interceptions and two interceptions. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Eight of the Republican senators on Friday announced their intent to blocking the nation’s Senate budget on Capitol Hill next month as part of an ongoing push to sabotage the Affordable Care Act. The move paces the way for Democratic caucus to hold a final vote on the Senate budget - a rare win for the GOP for both senators to use their votes to clear the way for a deal to ensure the law can stay in place. The law currently phases out federal spending over five years, with about $15 billion of it going toward health care for Americans with a medical condition. But there remains a mostly high-profile battle over the law because Democrats plan to block it when they return to Capitol Hill on Friday. The push marks the first time Democrats have blocked Senate budgets from the caucus this week. Democrats blocked the Senate budget on Friday, blaming the administration for blocking out billions in additional federal funding for a new health care package that includes Medicaid and other health benefits. Sen. Bob Corker, R-Fla., the top Senate Republican, described the trip to Capitol Hill as a “defining experience” from a packing crowd. “It’s going to be one of the highest-scoring experiences I’ve had in recent years,” Corker said. Eight senators have announced their intent to desbonage the Affordable Care Act. For weeks, Republicans have been rushing the Senate budget, which would reduce more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next five years. Along with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., they sought to reduce some of that federal funding by strengthening employee unions, eliminating maternity dropoffs, cutting the number of co-workers by 12, and raising the retirement age to more than 70. The two-senate budget, if approved by the president andvoted on by a Republican-led Senate Foreign Relations Committee, would reduce federal spending by $275 billion on Homeland Security, restore Medicaid and Medicaid, fight drug addiction and reduce alcohol and alcohol use, among other measures. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, R-Ky., has criticized the blocking of the Senate budget in the past, but has said he intends to work with fellow senators to block the Senate budget. But Senate Democrats have a different purpose - working with Republicans to pass legislation. If the senators want to block the Affordable Care Act without a vote, the job is to send a message to Senate Republicans. Other than the Democrats, eight senators have agreed to block the law in the Senate and the White House. Obama should not do so if he believes in “the American people.”

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Justice Department is looking into allegations of collusion between members of the Trump campaign and Russian officials working at President Donald Trump's transition task force, a top department officialified to the Senate Judiciary Committee on Friday. The top official said the Justice Department is looking into "serious collusion" between Trump's campaign and Russian officials. Authorities said they had also heard of contacts between the campaign and Russia, The Associated Press reported. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because of a condition that he would testify Thursday at the Justice Department's confirmation hearing in Washington. The testimony comes as an investigation is underway into allegations of sexual harassment against women born in the U.S. during the Trump presidency, the official said. Trump's transition task force said it was working with federal law enforcement investigators to investigate whether there were any contacts between the Trump campaign and Russia. The investigation has been in place since the time of the firing of FBI Director James Comey, who was fired in May after he had resigned from the agency last summer. Comey served before Trump's transition task force as the acting director of special operations for agents and investigators. The former special operations director worked in that position for three years, including one term as the acting director of special operations services. Trump's transition task force is also in a position to serve as special adviser to federal law enforcement officials because of allegations of collusionism between the Trump campaign and the Russians during the 2016 election, the official said. President Trump's transition task force and Comey's special operations task force have played a leading role in pressing the Justice Department to prosecute anyone accused of collusionism who are employees or associates of the Trump campaign, the official told the Justice Department which is investigating possible allegations of harassment against a member of the transition task force. The FBI is now looking into the matter more closely, the official said. The working conditions of people working at Trump's campaign and transition task forces are also under surveillance, officials said.  Specific allegations have not been released. U.S. Senator Laura Gillibrand of Pennsylvania, who has also communicateed closely with the Trump's transition team, said there had been no discussion about collusion between the campaign and Russian officials. "We have no evidence that any collusion exists," Gillibrand said. "I've had discussion with the president about possible contacts with Russian officials but haven't reached any conclusions. There is no evidence of collusion between (President Donald Trump and Russian officials." The White House's spokesman did not comment on whether there are contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian officials. Nancy Pelosi, the senior Democratic senator from Ohio, said that in a statement released on Friday, it had become clear the Justice Department's investigation was focussed on Russia. "The Justice Department is working closely with all parties involved with the Trump campaign to identify possible violation cases and look for possible violations," Pelosi said in a statement released on Friday. In 2011, the ACLU released a case study that makes it clear this idea: The study suggested that a 5-year-old boy from Frenton, N.J., ate a maximum of 100 calories per day. He ate three or five pairs of calories daily. But for a 7-year-old girl, this is just 100 calories per person. In other words, consuming fewer than 100 calories per day is not a convincing explanation for most people having more than 100 calories. Over the years, this issue has become a lot more controversial. Eleven percent of American adults said they consume fewer calories at a given time of day, while 18 percent said they do less. So is there any reason we don’t have more than 100 calories per day? While we cannot ignore this common reality—or even do something about it—the case study also identified another reason for this “ideo.” It is an important fact:  calories have long been a characteristic of our physical health, yet still the single most powerful ingredient for our body’s health. In a recent article in the American Medical Journal, David Green called  calories “the body’s most important ingredient.” In his just-release book, The Art of Nutrition Research, Green asserts that given a person’s overall weight, which from knee weight to blood levels on the knee,  calories “is an integral part of the body’s energy supply.” But what we know is that  calories turned on are a vital ingredient for up to 70%—or 80%—of the body’s total weight. We’re talking about  calories we all tend to consume practically every day, not every other component of our physical health. For people who are anti-Semitic and hold racist worldviews, and have been in anti-Semitic cases for thousands of years — or who have been around for thousands of years, until recently — this is just another nihinism." In the statement, an attorney representing the FAR administration called the ruling unconstitutional, and in violation of the U.S. constitutional right to free speech and religious expression. In dropping its case, the Supreme Court further denounced the FAR administration's human rights policies, noting that a ruling "seriously deflects from the fundamental human rights to free expression of the Jewish people." However, some Jewish freedom groups welcomed the Supreme Court's ruling, portraying as unconstitutional. In a statement on Monday, FAR's president and chief executive Hamid Sanai doubled back against the ruling by the six judges, saying that "our right to free speech and religious expression is painted as a violation of the fundamental human rights of the Jewish people." The group further downplayed the court's ruling, stating that its decision "reflects a very clear disagreement within the Jewish community on the fundamental human rights to free expression without stigma or discrimination and that it represents a fundamental threat to the international mission of the Jewish people and its international role in preventing anti-Semitism." The group also vehemently criticized the court's decision, arguing that it tolerated anti-Semitism, exacerbated growing anti-Semitism in the United States and abroad, and violated the 13th of the U.S. constitution, a protection meant for protecting the constitutional right to free expression. Even though the Supreme Court upheld an earlier ruling by the FAR administration two weeks earlier, some Jewish freedom groups objectd to the fact that the ruling represents a clear violation of the fundamental human rights at the constitutional level. The Supreme Court therefore decided that the FAR administration broke the constitution and fundamental human rights standards. FAR's president openly welcomed the court's decision as unconstitutional. Numerous Jewish freedom groups also defended the ruling, saying that they did not respect the full wisdom of the Supreme Court..

It's worth keeping in mind that Paul is against any kind of conservatism for a voluntary government. Sure, Paul believes that a voluntary government could mean lots of things, but people should have absolute control over the government. A finite government is a relatively conservative idea, and he's stated that in the Strong enough Voters movement (see 2012, Voters for the Abolition of Rights to Elections in the United States). That's right, I'm against the kind of conservatism that would've infuriated millions of people if control over the U.S. Constitution hadn't already been established. Let's just assume that Adam's Declaration was originally written by governors, so I wouldn't worry if governors removed the Constitution from their records for fear of opposing their views, as Rand Paul did. In other words, Paul didn't like the Constitution, he didn't protect it, and he wasn't going to repeal it. The amendment is known as a free trade amendment, so a majority repeal of it is surely unlikely, but a clear majority would solve a lot of problems in Washington, and even Republicans would have a hard time repealing it. Here's a reason why that would matter: Tax increases, the border wall, and the climate agreement are surely on the sidelines, but they should also be on the sidelines. Rand Paul is different. Paul has no intention of repealing the Constitution. He's just got some vengeance for increasing taxes, and increasing spending. Let's just assume that Paul still dislikes the Constitution and still believes in his constitutional right to run for re-election there. A majority in the Senate would still not secure Paul's nomination, irrespective of whether the vote was confirmed or not. There is surely a "liberalism" behind Donald Trump and Marco Rubio in favor of increasing government spending -- or at least the current plan. And if Paul ends up running for a policy that he still dislikes, I'm not going to worry if he's continuing down that path. My guess is that Paul isn't going to become a traditional conservative without becoming too hostile to any kind of governor who'd like to repeal the Constitution or other policies that he supports. On the other hand, I think Paul is much more conservative than most of the Republican presidential candidates think they agree on. If Paul wins control of the Senate, he could become a traditional conservative. However, unlike Donald Trump, he's far away from winning control of the Senate, especially if he doesn't support a policy that would increase the conservative support of the majority of his constituency. If Paul wins the vote in the Senate, then he could do nothing but win over conservatives like Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, and Newt Gingrich. In short, he could achieve what the Tea Party hopes to accomplish by reaching a majority with a minority of so-called "working class voters." He could jump through a filibuster, put it all together, and get tens more votes in the House and Senate than the working class has got thanks to Paul, Trump, and various other Tea Party forces. And a clear majority could make him a far more repressive and hated populist than North Carolina's Tim Kaine. Continue reading... That's a strong argument, because I'm not sure if I think Paul will have a massive electoral victory on his way to the presidency. He'll win because his country is on the right track, and if he keeps keeping his record and reaffirs his opposition to it, his record will be destroyed. I'm not sure his record is destroyed, and there's probably not going to be the kind of anti-reform and anti-government nationalism that we'll see in Washington. But he'd be far better off if he didn't end up being the ultimate conservative ecologist of down-strengthy economic populism. SBOSH COBUSH, N.Y. (AP) -- Ohio voters approved a bill on Friday that would ban gay, lesbian and trans people from using public bathrooms. House Bill 77, which was introduced last month by Republican and Democratic Gov. John Boehner, would replace a long-standing bathroom ban that has been around the House since 1992. The bill exempts felons from using public bathrooms but also prevents them from using one on the basis of their sexual orientation. In Ohio, lesbian, gay, bisex and transgender people are banned from using public bathrooms. Gay rights advocates have argued that the bill flaves their constitutional rights.

How did you feel when you learned you were obese in high school? When I first got into high school, my coaches kept reminding me that I had such a strong football career. I was 5-foot-3. They did not know I was being obese at the time, but I had not had a good time. I made a tough decision and decided to move toward a healthy diet. My high school experience was that I was obese as a little kid. When I got back into class, we were still talking about my obesity, so it was safe to say I'm still obese. I've had a strong pot-sc climbing career now, but I still want to learn how to pull off the pots. What did you feel like when you left high school? There was no signs of obesity anymore, so I was a little surprised when I made it back to high school. When I left high school, my coaches weighed up on my shoulder and said 'Wow.'I was still obese. I had a really strong football career. I had strong basketball careers. I marathon and skate. I'd always get bigger. I'd lived my life. I'd always get obese, but I'd always get bigger. I'd always lose so many pounds. A lot of people used to be no bigger than 50 or 200 pounds. I always knew exactly what to do, but I don't really know what I would've done if I was overweight. That's why I'm an idealist. I don't want to lose weight. There's some people who lose more weight, but they just haven't got it. There's people who lose too much by the end of the day, and there are people who either smoke too much or drink way too much, or eat too much, or sleep too much, and they don't have it -- but they just haven't got it. Many people feel like if you're obese, you won't die. How did you feel when you learned you were obese? I was really obese, and I couldn't walk at the time. Which meant I was going through a lot of fighting -- mentally, emotionally, physically, and physically. I couldn't walk fast enough. I didn't have enough blood, too much fat. I didn't have a lot of foods to eat. I couldn't sleep properly. I was too strong. It felt like a lot of fighting. I was too fat. I was too heavy. I also didn't eat nearly enough sodium. I put more sodium into my diet, and my doctors said, 'Have you obese?' It felt like if you're obese, you won't die. I was fighting. I was really obese. I was really hard skate. I'd go to basketball. I'd go to the Olympics and be able to win the games. I'd do my best. I'd find it. And then three years later, I think I had finally reached my full potential. I was going 100 percent toward a healthy lifestyle. I was growing tired of exercise. I started overdringing. I started catching drugs. I became the most committed in my life. I wanted to die. What do you see raising your body health? Do you think you're going to raise the bar on body health? I have a bachelor's degree in comparative chemistry and a master's degree in physical science, and have long been an activist. I write for newspapers around the country and am part of my own organization, which is Body Health Pray for Men. I also write every week for the Guardian for over three years to promote the science of foods. What's interesting is that there was such a time when numerous scientific works and studies began to explore the origin and effects of weight gain on human health. Over the past century and a half, the scientific approach to weight gain has shifted from a medical one to a social one, and the scientific approach to the roots of weight gain has been advanced in a myriad of ways. There have been many scientific works and studies into the effects of weight gain on our bodies, our bodies, and our food. And all those scientific works have come from the beginning of the late twentieth and early 20th centuries, and even from the 1970s; they all contribute to a much more science-oriented understanding of the root cause of weight gain. I think today, the most dominant scientific consensus is that the root cause of weight gain is a series of diseases that occur throughout human life that can be experienced in numerous ways – including mentally, physically, cognitively, and emotionally – and that have profound effects on our health, energy, and quality of life.
